wine.name: Barbaresco
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, granted to Barbaresco in 1980
wine.grapes: Nebbiolo alone, as the appellation requires.
wine.sites: Fourteen of the family's own vineyards around the village of Barbaresco, each picked and fermented on its own before the blend.
wine.making: Each vineyard is fermented apart in stainless steel. The wines then spend a year in barriques, a share of them new French oak, before they are blended, and a second year in large oak casks before bottling.
wine.glass: Red cherry, rose petal and liquorice with a touch of clove and tar; pale garnet, polished and fresh, with firm, fine grained tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Opens from about eight years after the vintage and keeps developing for two decades or more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: The family name, printed large across the top of the label.
The DOCG for Nebbiolo from the Barbaresco zone, aged at least twenty six months, nine of them in wood.

records.table: Gaja's Barbaresco is the house's village wine: Nebbiolo from fourteen family vineyards around Barbaresco, each fermented apart, then a year in barriques and a year in large casks. Polished, perfumed and firm, it wants decanting and a large glass.
records.story: In 1859 the founder of the house began to make and sell wine in the village of Barbaresco, and five generations of the family have followed him there. The change came when the founder's great grandson joined in 1961. He brought French barriques into the cellar and, from the 1967 vintage, bottled single vineyards on their own: Sorì San Lorenzo first, then Sorì Tildìn in 1970 and Costa Russi in 1978. That same year he planted Cabernet Sauvignon on a Nebbiolo site in the village, and his father's verdict, darmagi, what a pity, gave the wine its name. From the 1996 vintage the three single vineyard wines left the Barbaresco DOCG and were sold as Langhe Nebbiolo, so that a little Barbera could join the blend; with the 2013 vintage, under the next generation, they returned to Barbaresco as Nebbiolo alone. Through all of it the village wine, a blend of the family's parcels raised first in barrique and then in large casks, stayed the house's calling card. For a sommelier it is the Gaja to know first: the family name printed large across the label, and Barbaresco beneath it.

wine.name: Barolo Riserva Monfortino
wine.classification: Riserva: at least sixty two months of ageing before release, eighteen of them in wood
wine.sites: The Francia vineyard in Serralunga d'Alba, bought by the family in 1974 and the source of every Monfortino from 1978; from the 2015 vintage a selection from Arione, in the same commune, joins it.
wine.making: Only in years the family judges worthy, a selection of the Francia grapes is fermented apart in open topped wooden vats without temperature control, with up to five weeks on the skins. The wine then ages for some seven years in large Slavonian oak casks, against about four for the house's other Barolo, before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, dried rose and orange peel over tar, iron and leather, with a note of liquorice; pale for its power, with towering, fine grained tannin, high acidity and a very long finish.
wine.ageing: Released only after years in cask, it wants a further decade or more in bottle in a strong vintage and lasts for many decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: Named for Monforte d'Alba, the family's home village, though the grapes grow in Serralunga d'Alba.

records.table: Monfortino is Giacomo Conterno's Barolo Riserva, made only in years the family judges worthy, from the Francia vineyard in Serralunga, fermented long in open wooden vats and aged some seven years in large casks. Decant it well and expect it to need time.
records.story: The house traces its beginnings, by most accounts, to 1908, when the family opened a tavern near Monforte d'Alba and sold its own wine there. After the First World War the founder's son, whose name the house bears, set aside a Barolo for long ageing; first bottled, by most accounts, in the 1920s, it took the name Monfortino from his home village, and until 1978 it was made from bought grapes. He passed the firm to his two sons, and in 1969 the younger left to found his own estate, Poderi Aldo Conterno, while the elder kept the family name. In 1974 the elder brother bought Cascina Francia, a farm in Serralunga d'Alba, and from the 1978 vintage Monfortino came only from it. His own son took over the cellar at his death, and from the 2015 vintage a selection from Arione, in the same commune, has joined Francia. The method has changed little: a long fermentation in open wooden vats, years in large Slavonian casks, and a decision each year whether Monfortino will be made at all. For a sommelier it is traditional Barolo at its slowest: released late, built to be kept, and named for a village its grapes no longer come from.

wine.name: Barolo
wine.sites: Four sites blended into one wine: Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rué in the commune of Barolo, and Rocche dell'Annunziata in La Morra.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented with native yeasts in concrete vats, followed by a long maceration on the skins. The Barolo then rests for some two and a half to three years in large Slavonian oak casks, never in barrique, before bottling.
wine.glass: Pale garnet, with rose petal, sour cherry and tar over dried orange peel and a hint of liquorice; lifted and fragrant rather than dense, with firm, dusty tannin and bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first decade, it opens at ten to fifteen years and lasts for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: The name the cellar took in Bartolo's time; older labels read Cantina Mascarello.
The DOCG for Nebbiolo from the Barolo zone, aged at least thirty eight months, eighteen of them in wood.

records.table: Bartolo Mascarello makes one Barolo, blending Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rué in Barolo with Rocche dell'Annunziata in La Morra, fermented in concrete and aged in large Slavonian casks, never barrique. Pale, fragrant and firm, it rewards patience and decanting.
records.story: Bartolo's father built the cellar in the village of Barolo in 1919, though one account has him making Barolo a year earlier, and sold his wine as Cantina Mascarello. Bartolo joined him in 1945 and learned the trade from him. The family blended its vineyards into one Barolo, as the old houses of the village did: Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rué in Barolo, and Rocche dell'Annunziata across the hill in La Morra. From the 1980s many neighbours turned to single vineyard bottlings, shorter macerations and new French barriques. Bartolo refused all three and became an outspoken voice of tradition in what came to be called the Barolo Wars. Late in life he painted labels by hand, and one that read No Barrique, No Berlusconi, aimed at new oak and at the prime minister of the day, became a collector's piece in the early 2000s. He died in March 2005, aged seventy eight, and his daughter took over and kept his methods. For a sommelier the wine is an argument in a bottle: that Barolo is a blend of places and of patience, and that the commune can matter more than the cru.

wine.name: Barolo Le Rocche del Falletto Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva, declared only in years the house judges exceptional and marked by a red label
wine.sites: Le Rocche, the upper part of the Falletto amphitheatre in Serralunga d'Alba, facing south to south west on calcareous clay; the family bought Falletto in the early 1980s.
wine.making: Fermented and macerated on the skins in vat, the wine is aged for close to three years in large casks of French oak, then held in bottle for two years and more before it is released as a Riserva.
wine.glass: Rose petal, red cherry and tar over liquorice, dried orange peel and a hint of white truffle; taut and perfumed, with high acidity and fine but very firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Closed for ten years and more, it opens slowly through its second decade and lasts for decades after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large, wide bowled glass.

records.table: Bruno Giacosa's Le Rocche del Falletto Riserva is Nebbiolo from the upper part of the family's own Falletto vineyard in Serralunga, aged close to three years in large casks and released under the red label only in chosen years. Decant it and give it time.
records.story: Bruno Giacosa (1929 to 2018) was born in Neive and began working in the family cellar at thirteen, beside his father and grandfather, in a family business that made wine from bought grapes. For decades he did the same, choosing fruit from growers he knew vineyard by vineyard, and from the 1964 vintage he bottled a Barbaresco from Santo Stefano in Neive under the name of its site, one of the early wines of a single vineyard in the Langhe. In the early 1980s he bought his first vineyard, Falletto, an amphitheatre of calcareous clay in Serralunga d'Alba, and the wines of his own vines took a second name, Azienda Agricola Falletto, beside the Casa Vinicola that bought grapes. The upper part of the hill, Le Rocche, gave the Barolo he held back in years he judged exceptional and released as a Riserva under a red label; in other years it wore the white. He added parcels in Asili and Rabajà in Barbaresco in the late 1990s. He died in January 2018 at eighty eight, and his daughter carried the house on. For a sommelier the red label is the sign to know: a Riserva kept for years when the vineyard and the season both deserved it.

wine.name: Barbaresco
wine.sites: A blend of the members' vineyards across the commune of Barbaresco, whose named crus include Asili, Rabajà, Montestefano, Ovello and Pora.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel at about 28 degrees Celsius, with some four weeks on the skins and pumping over two or three times a day. The wine then ages for twenty months to two years, as the vintage decides, in large oak casks of fifty hectolitres.
wine.glass: Red cherry, rose and raspberry over tar, liquorice and dried orange peel; pale garnet, fresh and savoury, with firm, fine tannin and a clean finish.
wine.ageing: Drinks from about five years after the vintage and keeps well for fifteen to twenty in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large, wide bowled glass.

label.means: The producers of Barbaresco: the village's growers' cooperative, founded in 1958.
The DOCG for Nebbiolo from the Barbaresco zone, aged at least twenty six months, nine of them in wood.

records.table: Produttori del Barbaresco is the village cooperative, and its Barbaresco blends the members' Nebbiolo from across the commune, fermented in steel and aged about two years in large casks. Fresh, perfumed and honest, it is the Barbaresco to teach the appellation with.
records.story: Barbaresco's first cooperative cellar was set up in the village castle in 1894 by the head of Alba's royal school of oenology, who gathered a small group of growers around him. The cellar did not long outlive him, and in the 1920s, as fascism took hold, it was shut. In 1958 the parish priest, worried that families were leaving the land, brought nineteen growers together to found the Produttori del Barbaresco. The opening vintage was made in the yard beside his house with second hand equipment, and most of it was sold in bulk to pay for a cellar, finished in 1960 at the foot of the village tower. From the 1967 vintage the cooperative bottled its first single vineyard wines, Asili, Ovello, Pora and Moccagatta among them; they grew into nine Riserve, made only in vintages judged excellent and released after four years. Barbaresco became a DOC in 1966 and a DOCG in 1980. The plain Barbaresco carries the members' fruit from across the commune. For a sommelier it is how the appellation is taught: one village, one grape and many growers, in a bottle a guest can open young.
